better: I have a question.
why: In India 'doubt' often means a question. Elsewhere it means you suspect something is untrue, so a teacher abroad may think you disbelieve them.

better: Please do what is needed. (Or say exactly what: 'Please approve the leave.')
why: Common in Indian offices, but it sounds old-fashioned and vague elsewhere. Naming the action is clearer and politer.

better: I will reply by evening.
why: Outside India, 'revert' means 'go back to an earlier state', not 'reply'. Use 'reply', 'get back to you' or 'respond'.

better: Can we bring the meeting forward?
why: 'Prepone' is a neat Indian word, the opposite of 'postpone'. Most people outside India have never heard it, so say 'bring forward'.

better: He is out of town. / He is away.
why: 'Out of station' comes from British-era India, where an officer's posting was his 'station'. It is fine at home, but 'out of town' or 'away' is understood everywhere.

better: He is my cousin.
why: English 'cousin' covers both boys and girls. Indian English adds 'brother' or 'sister' to show gender; outside India, people simply say 'cousin'.

say: I passed out of IIT in 2019.
better: I graduated from IIT in 2019.
why: In India 'pass out' means finish a course. Elsewhere it usually means to faint, which can cause a funny moment in an interview.

say: Let us discuss about the budget.
better: Let us discuss the budget.
why: 'Discuss' already means 'talk about', so it takes no 'about'. You can say 'talk about the budget' or 'discuss the budget'.

say: I will return back on Monday.
better: I will return on Monday. / I will be back on Monday.
why: 'Return' already means 'come back', so 'back' repeats the idea. Keep one of them.

better: Can you repeat it? / Can you say it again?
why: 'Repeat' already means 'say again'. 'Repeat it again' would strictly mean a third time.

say: I have lived here since two years.
better: I have lived here for two years.
why: Use 'for' with a length of time (for two years) and 'since' with a starting point (since 2023, since Diwali).

better: I met her this morning.
why: This comes from Hindi 'aaj subah'. Standard English says 'this morning', 'this afternoon', 'this evening' and 'tonight'.

better: I called you last night.
why: Standard English says 'last night', though 'yesterday morning' and 'yesterday evening' are fine.

say: The updation of records is pending.
better: The updating of records is pending. / The records have not been updated yet.
why: 'Updation' is widely used in Indian offices but is not found in most dictionaries outside India. 'Update' or 'updating' works everywhere.

better: I have a car.
why: Verbs of owning, like 'have' for possession, usually do not take '-ing'. 'I am having lunch' is fine, because that is an action.

better: He knows the answer.
why: 'Know', 'understand', 'believe' and 'want' describe states, not actions, so standard English rarely uses them with '-ing'.

better: I am Rahul. / My name is Rahul.
why: 'Myself' is used when the subject acts on itself ('I hurt myself'). To introduce yourself, say 'I am' or 'My name is'.

better: May I ask your name?
why: A warm, polite translation of 'aapka shubh naam'. Outside India it can sound puzzling, as if you have a bad name too.

better: Where are you staying?
why: 'Put up' for 'stay' is old British usage kept alive in India. 'Where are you staying?' is understood everywhere today.

better: He is my wife's sister's husband.
why: A useful Indian word for a relation English has no single word for. Outside India, explain the relation or say 'brother-in-law'.

better: You're welcome. / Don't mention it.
why: A polite Indian reply to 'thank you'. Elsewhere, 'You're welcome', 'No problem' or 'Don't mention it' are the usual answers.

say: I can't cope up with the work.
better: I can't cope with the work.
why: The phrase is 'cope with'. The 'up' probably comes from 'keep up with' and 'catch up with'.

say: The team comprises of five people.
better: The team comprises five people. / The team consists of five people.
why: 'Comprise' needs no 'of'. Use 'comprises five' or 'consists of five' or 'is made up of five'.

say: Write your name in capital alphabets.
better: Write your name in capital letters.
why: The 'alphabet' is the whole set of letters, A to Z. Each one is a 'letter'.

better: I need it today, please. / I need it by the end of today.
why: 'Itself' adds emphasis in Indian English, like Hindi 'aaj hi'. Elsewhere it sounds odd; use 'today', 'this very day' or a clear deadline.

better: I'm right here.
why: 'Only' as emphasis comes from Hindi 'yahin'. Outside India it can sound like 'I am here and nowhere else'. 'Right here' keeps the emphasis.

say: You are coming tomorrow, isn't it?
better: You are coming tomorrow, aren't you?
why: Indian English often uses 'isn't it?' after any sentence, like 'na?'. Standard English matches the tag to the verb: 'aren't you?', 'didn't she?'.

better: I will be there by 5. / I'll reach the office by 5.
why: 'Would' sounds uncertain or conditional abroad, as if something might stop you. Use 'will'. Also, 'reach' usually needs a place after it.
